name: Media Lengua
confidence_why: Every description agrees on fixed penultimate stress that shifts rightward as suffixes are added, from Muysken 1997 as reported in Stewart, Prado Ayala and Gonza Inlago 2020 to the instrumental confirmation in Onosson and Stewart 2021, with Stewart 2011 and Stewart 2015 consistent; the only qualification is Onosson and Stewart's remark that the prominence is carried by pitch rather than intensity, and almost all of the evidence comes from one fieldworker's Pijal corpus, with Muysken's own text not consulted.

catalog_quote: Prosody, most notably intonation, has also been investigated in Media Lengua. Muysken (1997) identifies that, like Quichua, Media Lengua makes use of penultimate stress, which consistently shifts as suffixes are added to a word (16). (16) vaca [ˈbaka] vacagu [baˈkaɡu] vacagucuna [bakaɡuˈkuna] vacagucunamanta [bakaɡukunaˈmanta] vacagucunamantami [bakaɡukunamanˈtami] vaca-gu-cuna-manta-mi cow-DIM-PL-ABL-VAL ‘from the little cows’ (based on Stewart, 2015) Stewart’s (2015) analysis of Media Lengua intonation looks at pitch accents and confirms that they are ... realized in the same position as stressed syllables described by Muysken (1997). The most common realization being a low-high pitch accent (L+H*) taking place at the prosodic word level on, leading up to, or just after the penultimate syllable of a word. new_statements.quote: p. 8: "Media Lengua, like Quichua, has fixed stress on the penultimate syllable, which ‘shifts’ to the new penultimate syllable when its suffixing agglutinating morphology is added e.g., [ˈɡato] ‘cat’ ⟹ [ɡaˈtota] ‘cat-acc’ ⟹ [ɡatoˈtami] ‘cat-acc-val.’" p. 19: "Evidence from Stewart (2015a) supports these findings, which describes a bitonal pitch accent ending a high target (L+H*) on the penultimate syllable." ... "The lack of a strong correlation between stress and intensity may suggest that the term ‘pitch accent’ more aptly reflects the differences in syllable quality between penultimate position and non-penultimate position than ‘stress,’ which is typically used in the Quechuan literature." p. 20 n. 9: "Media Lengua stress/pitch-accent is normally carried on the penultimate syllable"

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate). Refines it with the shifting-under-suffixation examples, the acoustic correlates (f0, vowel fronting, no intensity effect) and the pitch accent characterisation; describes the Pijal (Imbabura) variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word as a whole and moves rightward as suffixes are added; phonetically it is realised mainly as an L+H* pitch rise (about 9 Hz higher f0 on the stressed syllable) with fronting of the stressed vowel, and little intensity difference, so the authors suggest 'pitch accent' may be the better label than 'stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Three stressed open-final tokens in the corpus are called exceptional (p. 20 n. 9); a full account of stress patterning is said to be beyond the paper's scope.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources actually read (Stewart 2011, Stewart 2015, Onosson & Stewart 2021) describe Pijal Media Lengua (Imbabura province, northern Ecuador), whereas the listed Muysken 1997 chapter describes Salcedo Media Lengua (Cotopaxi); the catalog record does not name a variety. Onosson & Stewart 2021 state the penultimate pattern holds for Media Lengua 'like Quichua' generally.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: every opened source has Media Lengua stress on the penultimate syllable of the suffixed word, matching the catalog rule. Two nuances: (a) Onosson & Stewart 2021 argue the phenomenon is realised as an L+H* pitch accent with almost no intensity correlate and suggest 'pitch accent' may be the apter term than 'stress', so a reader could file it as pitch accent-like, but the placement is fixed penultimate either way; (b) Stewart 2011 shows Spanish loans with non-Quichua stress entering Pijal Media Lengua, yet the transcribed PML forms are all penultimate (patrón -> ˈpat.ɾon), so no counterexample to the rule appears. The listed work (Muysken 1997) could not be opened, so whether the Salcedo variety is described identically is unverified from the primary text.

tone.quote: In the tradition of metrical phonology, Pijal Media Lengua is a quantity insensitive language and like most Quechuan languages, has fixed primary stress2 (henceforth pitch accent) on the penultimate syllable of a word. ... In nearly every utterance type in this dataset (declaratives, questions, exclamatives, vocatives and imperatives), a bitonal L+H* pitch accent is realized as a rising pitch movement associated with the penultimate syllable of a prosodic word (pw) in both nuclear and prenuclear configurations.
tone.summary: Acoustic ToBI intonation study: 'pitch accent' and 'tone' are intonational (AM) terms here - an L+H* accent on the fixed penultimate accented syllable, H*/emphatic accents, L%/H% boundary tones. Nothing on lexical tone, present or absent. Fn. 2: 'accent' replaces 'stress' since only F0 is analysed.
